name: Chromium DOM Distiller (chromium/dom-distiller, `domdistiller.js`). Surfaces as Chrome Reader Mode / 'Show simplified view' on Android, the desktop `#enable-reader-mode` flag and `--enable-dom-distiller`, and the iOS Reading List. Ports: go-domdistiller (markusmobius). Associated Chromium components: DistillabilityAgent, DistillabilityService, DistillablePageDetector, the `chrome-distiller://` scheme.
kind: Browser feature, implemented as a library. Written in Java, compiled to JavaScript via GWT with Apache Ant, and shipped as a prebuilt JS blob in the Chromium tree at third_party/dom_distiller_js/dist/. It is therefore simultaneously a standalone extractor and a piece of browser plumbing, and the two have different properties -- most published discussion conflates them.
maturity: Deprecated in effect, though never formally announced as such. The chromium/dom-distiller repository was ARCHIVED on 2 February 2023 and is read-only; the compiled artifact still ships in Chromium and Reader Mode still functions, but the extractor is frozen. Desktop Reader Mode never left the flag/experimental state across many years. The GWT-and-Ant toolchain is itself effectively dead, which means the archived source is not practically rebuildable without archaeology. Treat it as a frozen reference implementation, not as a dependency.
license: BSD-3-Clause (the Chromium license). Permits use here without restriction. Note the practical caveat: what is usable is the compiled `domdistiller.js` artifact, since rebuilding from the archived Java/GWT source requires a toolchain nobody maintains -- so 'adopting' it in practice means vendoring a frozen 2023 JavaScript blob.
keeps_and_discards: A three-stage pipeline documented in Chromium's own accessibility docs: (1) hidden elements are removed from the examination set; (2) remaining elements are labelled 'content' or 'not content' based on word count, RELATIVE PAGE POSITION, and IMAGE DIMENSIONS; (3) the content-labelled elements are concatenated into simplified HTML. Underneath, the algorithm is loosely based on Boilerpipe (Kohlschuetter, Fankhauser and Nejdl, 2009) -- text-density and link-density block classification -- with Chromium-specific additions layered on: a DomConverter that lowers the live DOM into an internal WebDocument model, a filtering/sanitization pass, a separate metadata extractor, a content-image collector, and a PaginationSystem that detects next/previous page links and can stitch multi-page articles. Kept: article prose, headings, in-article images with their dimensions, tables and figures, and the title/author/date metadata. Discarded: navigation, footers, sidebars, comments, ads, all form controls, and anything the visibility pass judges hidden. Crucially the keep/discard decision uses SPATIAL information -- position on the page and image size -- which no other extractor in this batch does.
structure_preserved: Better than a text extractor, worse than it looks. Output is a DOM tree, not a string: DOM Distiller's whole premise is 'traverse the DOM and return a clean DOM tree', so nesting, document order, headings, lists, tables and figures survive as real elements, and images survive with dimensions attached. The result is delivered as a DomDistillerResult protocol buffer carrying distilled HTML, title, content_images, pagination_info and timing/debug fields. What is destroyed: the ancestor chain above kept content (output is reparented into the distiller's own page template), element identity, all attributes not needed for rendering, and every relation between kept and discarded material. Shadow boundaries: this is the interesting case in this batch, because DOM Distiller runs INSIDE the page against a live DOM, so it could in principle see open shadow roots -- but its DomConverter walks light-DOM children, so open shadow content is missed anyway, and it predates widespread shadow DOM entirely (frozen 2023, designed ~2014). No unreachable marker is emitted, so shadow-heavy pages silently distil to almost nothing.
interactive_elements: Removed entirely. Form controls, buttons and inputs are all classified as not-content and dropped; the output is a reading artifact rendered at a `chrome-distiller://` URL where scripts do not run at all, so even surviving markup would be inert. Links survive as anchors within the distilled body. The pagination system is the one place controls are treated as meaningful -- it identifies next/previous page links as navigational affordances rather than boilerplate -- and that is a narrowly-scoped exception: it recognises exactly one affordance type, for exactly one purpose, and discards the rest.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero, and enforced twice over. The elements carrying disabled/checked/selected/aria-expanded/aria-selected/aria-pressed/role are dropped in stage 2, and the destination context (`chrome-distiller://`, scripts disabled) could not honour interactive state even if it survived. aria attributes participate only in the hidden-element pass. The token cost of state is nil and the affordance count is nil. What makes DOM Distiller instructive rather than merely another zero is that it had the strongest possible position for preserving state -- live DOM, computed style, layout, full browser context, running before anything is serialized -- and used all of that budget to make a better READING artifact rather than a better ACTING artifact. It is the clearest available demonstration that the affordance gap in this field is a goal choice, not a capability limit.
layout_awareness: YES -- and this is the single most important fact about DOM Distiller and the reason it belongs in this batch. It is the only extractor here that reads geometry, and it reads it in two distinct places. (a) In the distiller: element importance is scored partly on 'relative page position' and 'image dimensions', which are geometric quantities, and the hidden-element pass runs against a live DOM with computed style available (display, visibility, and element size), not merely against inline attributes. (b) In the browser integration: the DistillabilityAgent runs in the renderer and is TRIGGERED BY LAYOUT -- 'whenever the compositor makes a meaningful change to the layout, which happens 1 to 3 times as the page loads'. Geometry is therefore not a peripheral read by an actuator; it is the clock and it is inside the classification. That is the exact inversion of this project's no_layout_in_the_fold constraint, which makes DOM Distiller the definitive negative control for it: it shows what layout-in-the-fold buys (a materially better hidden-content filter, and a size-aware image decision) and what it costs (a fold that cannot run without a rendering engine, cannot run before layout, and re-runs on every relayout).
javascript_required: Yes, unavoidably and in both directions. It is itself JavaScript injected into the page, and it runs after load against the rendered DOM, so by the time it executes the page's own scripts have already run, its analytics have already fired, and its subresources have already loaded. There is no static-HTML mode. The consequence for a telemetry-conscious reader is that DOM Distiller offers no protection whatsoever at read time -- the page has fully executed. Notably, the privacy-motivated alternative in this space, Brave's SpeedReader (arXiv 1811.03661), was designed specifically to invert this: classify distillability from the URL and raw response BEFORE rendering, so the reading artifact is produced without ever executing the page. That inversion is the design lesson, and it is a real one -- SpeedReader demonstrates that a reader can be either layout-aware or telemetry-free, and DOM Distiller chose the former.
evaluation_method: There is no published fidelity evaluation from Google. Correctness inside Chromium is enforced by unit tests over the Java sources and by the distillability heuristics being tuned against internal page sets that were never released. Externally, DOM Distiller appears as one of the compared extractors in the Webis reproducibility study (Bevendorff, Gupta, Kiesel, Stein, 'An Empirical Comparison of Web Content Extraction Algorithms', SIGIR 2023), which unifies eight prior extraction datasets and scores with ROUGE-LSum and Levenshtein distance -- a sequence-based metric that, unlike word-bag F1, does penalise reordering. It is absent from WCXB's 2026 leaderboard and absent from Trafilatura's evaluation table, so its modern standing is undocumented. The separate and more interesting evaluated object is the DISTILLABILITY classifier, which is a binary decision (offer Reader Mode or not) evaluated as a classification problem against human judgements of 'is this an article', on data Google has not published.
corpus_size_and_origins: Unknown and unpublished for Google's own tuning; the distillability heuristics were trained/tuned on internal Chrome-scale data with no released size, origin count, date or sampling frame. This is the least transparent evidence base in the batch. The external figures inherit the SIGIR 2023 merge of eight legacy datasets -- CleanEval (2006-2007), L3S-GN1 (621 Google News pages, 2010), Dragnet and similar -- so its median evaluated page is from roughly 2010, predating responsive layout, consent banners, SPAs and shadow DOM entirely. Since DOM Distiller was itself designed against the ~2014 web and frozen in 2023, tool and corpus are era-matched, which flatters it: it is being scored on the web it was built for. [uncertain] on its exact SIGIR 2023 placement, since the ACM PDF is paywalled and returned 403.
reported_precision_recall: No figures published by Google, at all. No figure in WCXB, none in Trafilatura's table. The only quantitative statements in circulation are from the Webis SIGIR 2023 study, whose numeric table I could not retrieve, so any precision/recall attributed to DOM Distiller here would be fabricated. What IS documented, qualitatively and by Chromium itself, is the failure boundary: 'many news articles are distillable', while the Wikipedia main page is explicitly given as non-distillable because it has multiple equally-important text areas. That is a candid admission that the model is one-main-content-region and that multi-region pages -- listings, portals, dashboards, search results, which is most of the interesting web and most of this project's target population -- are out of scope by design rather than by tuning. Mark every quantitative claim about DOM Distiller [uncertain]; there are almost none to quote.
independent_oracle: None, and the structure of the problem is worse here than elsewhere. Google publishes no oracle; the SIGIR 2023 oracle is human reference text sharing the one-main-content premise; and the distillability classifier's oracle is human judgement of 'is this an article', which is the same premise one level up. So both the extractor and the gate that decides whether to run it are validated against the same assumption they encode. The only assumption-free check available is behavioural and Chromium effectively performs it in production without recording it: users toggle Reader Mode off, or never see the offer because the DistillabilityAgent declined. That signal exists at browser scale and is not published. No oracle-free metric (recall against full capture, round-trip fixed point, compression at fixed recall) has been computed for it by anyone.
evidence_independence: Google has published no fidelity figure, so nothing attributed to DOM Distiller is vendor-run -- but that is not the reassurance it sounds like, because it means there is essentially no evidence base at all. The one external evaluation is the Webis SIGIR 2023 study, which is COMPETITOR-run in the same sense flagged elsewhere in this batch: the Webis group authored Resiliparse, which the same study evaluates. So DOM Distiller's only published numbers come from a group with a competing extractor in the comparison. There is no third party with no stake who has measured it. Its reputation rests on deployment scale (it shipped in Chrome for a decade) rather than on any measurement, and deployment scale is not evidence of extraction fidelity -- it is evidence that a gate was conservative enough to avoid embarrassment, which the DistillabilityAgent's job description confirms.
page_archetype_coverage: Effectively single-archetype by design, and unusually honest about it. Articles work; the documentation names news articles as the target. Everything else is handled by REFUSAL rather than by degraded output: the DistillabilityAgent declines to offer Reader Mode, using features including whether the URL contains keywords such as 'forum', '.php' or 'index', whether the markup carries Facebook Open Graph or Google AMP identifiers, and the number of '/' characters in the URL path, alongside text-and-link density. Those URL-shape features are worth pausing on -- they are page-type classification from the ADDRESS, not from the content, which is both a striking shortcut and a direct structure_agnosticism violation of a kind not seen elsewhere in this batch: it names a page a forum because of a substring in its URL. For a project keyed on `url : xpath : markdown : content`, this is a specific temptation to name and refuse, because the url component makes exactly this shortcut available.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Weakly documented and structurally English-biased. The Boilerpipe lineage means word-count and text-density features, which undercount CJK information per character in the same way every character-threshold heuristic does. The distillability URL heuristics are keyed on English tokens ('forum', 'index') and on Latin-script URL conventions. Running inside a browser gives it correct Unicode handling and correct bidi RENDERING for free -- a genuine advantage over the static parsers, since the output is a DOM rendered by the same engine, so RTL and complex scripts display correctly rather than being reserialized without isolation marks. That is a real point in favour of in-browser extraction generally and is worth carrying over: rendering fidelity for scripts is free when you never leave the browser. Whitespace-free segmentation is unaddressed in the scoring. [uncertain] on any measured non-English performance; none is published.
leaks_outward: Complex, and the only entry in this batch where extraction itself has a network footprint worth discussing. The distiller runs after full page load, so the page has already executed and reported everything it wanted to. Entering Reader Mode then RE-LOADS the document under the `chrome-distiller://` scheme, which the origin can observe server-side as a second request -- and because scripts do not run on the distilled page, an origin that ships an in-article analytics beacon will see the beacon stop while the user is still reading, a distinctive and detectable pattern. Subresources referenced by the distilled content (notably content_images) are fetched from the distilled context, with mixed-content and certificate-error subresources blocked. On iOS the Reading List path involves server-side distillation in some configurations, which discloses the URL to Google; the on-device Android/desktop path does not. [uncertain] on the current iOS server-side distillation behaviour, which has changed across versions and which I could not verify for 2026.
mechanism_detectability: Detectable, in several ways, and this is the field where DOM Distiller most clearly fails the posture this project requires. (1) The DistillabilityAgent runs on compositor layout changes and executes non-trivial DOM traversal 1-3 times during load; that is measurable as a timing side channel by a page instrumenting its own layout and long-task timings. (2) `domdistiller.js` is injected into the page context to run its traversal, so its presence is in principle observable to a page that watches for unexpected script activity or property access patterns. [uncertain] on the exact isolated-world isolation of the injection in current Chromium, which the accessibility docs explicitly decline to describe -- they call the distiller 'a black box' from Chrome's perspective. (3) The `chrome-distiller://` navigation and the cessation of script execution are directly observable server-side and by any beacon in the article body. (4) The scheme's host is a random string plus a URL hash, which is a deliberate anti-linkability measure and the one hardening choice present. Net: the technique announces itself, both to the page in-session and to the origin across requests, and it therefore fails the standard this project sets for the sensor -- while never touching attachShadow, which is the one specific tripwire it does not trip.
countermeasures: Two are present and both are narrow. First, the `chrome-distiller://` host is constructed from a random string combined with a hash of the URL, which prevents the distilled URL from being a stable, guessable, or cross-linkable identifier. Second, distillation is gated on SecurityLevel::SECURE, with mixed-content subresources and certificate-error subresources refused -- a genuine security posture that most extractors have no analogue for. Neither addresses detectability. The broader countermeasure in this design space is architectural rather than incremental: Brave's SpeedReader, which classifies before render so the page never executes, is the existence proof that a reader mode can be privacy-preserving, and it achieves that by giving up exactly the layout awareness DOM Distiller depends on.
measured_fidelity_cost: Unmeasured in every direction. Google publishes no figure for what distillation drops relative to the full page, no third party frames DOM Distiller's loss as a cost against a stated control, and there is no affordance-retention number. The one measurable quantity that exists in production and is not published is the distillability REFUSAL RATE -- the fraction of pages the DistillabilityAgent declines -- which is the honest version of the fidelity cost for a tool whose failure mode is refusal rather than error, and which Chrome could report and does not. Against this project's 80.9%-projection / 99.7%-capture pair, DOM Distiller's numbers would be roughly 0% affordance retention on the pages it accepts and 0% coverage on the pages it refuses, with the refusal set including essentially every non-article archetype.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded, with one partial and accidental exception. Consent banners, paywalls, login walls and CAPTCHA interstitials are not modelled and not flagged: a paywall teaser distils cleanly into what looks like a complete article. The accidental exception cuts the other way and is worth noting -- because the distiller runs post-render on the live page, a full-viewport consent overlay is PRESENT in the DOM it examines, and the position-and-size features may rank the overlay's text highly, so gated pages can distil to the consent copy itself rather than to the article. That is a loud failure where most tools have a silent one, but it is luck rather than design, and no gate-state field exists in DomDistillerResult. With roughly two-thirds of top sites presenting a consent interface, any corpus built from distilled pages mixes populations invisibly.
determinism: Weaker than every static extractor here, and for an instructive reason. The algorithm is deterministic, but its INPUT is not: it consumes a live, post-layout DOM whose content depends on when it ran relative to lazy loading, hydration, ad insertion, viewport size, device pixel ratio, and animation state. Because two of its features are geometric -- relative page position and image dimensions -- the same document at two viewport widths produces two different classifications. Same URL does not mean same input, and same input in the strict sense (identical DOM plus identical layout) is not reproducible in a live browser. Running the same page twice can and does yield different distillations. This is the concrete cost of layout-in-the-fold, and it is the strongest single argument for the project's no_layout_in_the_fold constraint: geometry makes the fold a function of the viewport rather than of the document.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts on more axes than anything else in this batch, and two of them are outside the tool. The distiller JS itself is frozen since the 2023 archive, which removes one axis. But the Blink layout engine underneath is not frozen: any change to layout, computed style resolution, image sizing, or lazy-load timing changes the geometric features the classifier reads, so distiller output moves with the BROWSER version even though the distiller code is byte-identical. Separately the DistillabilityAgent, the DistillabilityService and the trigger conditions live in Chromium proper and continue to change. So output is a function of (frozen distiller blob, Blink version, viewport, network timing) and only one of those four can be pinned by vendoring the blob. Any claim of cross-version determinism for a layout-reading extractor is unsupportable, and this is the concrete evidence for that general point.
reproducibility: Poor, and structurally so. To re-obtain a result you must pin the distiller blob (possible), the Chromium version (possible but heavy), the viewport and device pixel ratio (possible), and the page's network-timing-dependent DOM state (not possible against a live origin). The archived repository at least freezes the source, and the compiled artifact in the Chromium tree is versioned, so the CODE is reproducible even though the RESULT is not. There is no released evaluation corpus, no released tuning data, no published leaderboard entry to re-run. This is the worst reproducibility posture in the batch and it is caused by exactly the property that makes the tool interesting -- live-DOM, layout-aware operation.
failure_modes: (1) Refusal: the DistillabilityAgent declines and Reader Mode is never offered. This is the dominant outcome on the modern web and is a LOUD failure, which is rare and valuable. (2) Multi-region collapse: pages with several equally-important text areas distil to an arbitrary one -- Chromium names the Wikipedia main page as the canonical example. (3) Overlay capture: a consent or subscription overlay present at distillation time scores highly on position and size and is returned as content. (4) Lazy-load truncation: content not yet loaded when the distiller ran is simply absent, with no marker. (5) Shadow-DOM blindness: component-heavy pages distil to near-nothing because DomConverter walks light-DOM children. (6) Pagination stitching errors: the PaginationSystem follows a wrong next-link and concatenates unrelated content. (7) Toolchain death: the source cannot practically be rebuilt, so any bug found today is unfixable without replacing the tool.
failure_visibility: The best in the batch on the primary failure and no better than average on the rest -- and this asymmetry is the single most transferable idea here. Refusal is explicit: a separate agent decides distillability BEFORE distilling, and when it declines, the user sees no Reader Mode offer rather than seeing a bad distillation. Separating 'can I do this?' from 'do it' is the loud-failure architecture this project's posture calls for, and it is architecturally cheap: a gate that can say 'I decline' converts a class of silent quality failures into an explicit refusal. The rest degrades silently in the usual way -- no confidence score in the output, no count of discarded nodes, no marker for lazy-loaded or shadow content that was never seen, no indication that the returned region beat its runner-up by one point. And the gate has its own silent failure: a false refusal is invisible, so pages that would have distilled fine are simply never offered, with no telemetry published on the rate.
scale_limits: Not built for corpus scale and never used at it. It is per-tab, per-page, in-renderer, and runs on the user's device budget; there is no batch mode, no streaming, no CLI in the Chromium build. Cost per page is a DOM traversal plus geometry reads, and geometry reads are the expensive part because querying layout properties can force synchronous style and layout recalculation -- so the cost is not a clean traversal but a traversal interleaved with layout flushes. The DistillabilityAgent additionally re-runs its examination 1 to 3 times per page load on compositor layout changes, so the cost is multiplied by the number of meaningful relayouts, which is unbounded on a page that keeps mutating. go-domdistiller exists precisely because the original cannot be run server-side at scale.
delta_cost_model: None, and it is instructive that the ONE tool here with an incremental-looking trigger still has none. The DistillabilityAgent is event-driven on layout change, which superficially resembles a delta model -- but what it does on each event is re-examine the page WHOLESALE, so the trigger is incremental and the work is not. That is the specific anti-pattern an O(delta) claim has to avoid, and DOM Distiller is the clean example of it: layout-change-triggered whole-page recomputation, 1-3 times per load and more on dynamic pages. Every change class is outside any bound, and geometric dependence makes it worse than the static extractors, because changes that alter NO content at all -- a viewport resize, a font load reflowing a column, an ad slot filling and shifting positions -- change the feature values and can change the output. CSS-driven change, which is invisible to every static extractor, is here VISIBLE and therefore cost-bearing. Shadow mutations remain invisible. Declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse is outside its era entirely. [uncertain] on whether the agent debounces or coalesces layout events.
reanchoring_stability: No node identity in the output and no re-anchoring mechanism, but with one component the others lack: because it runs in-page against a live DOM, node identity IS available to it at the moment it runs -- it simply does not carry it through. The DomConverter lowers live nodes into an internal WebDocument model and the output is reserialized HTML with no xpath, no source node reference, no offsets and no content hashes. Two distillations of the same page cannot be aligned except by text diff. What it does carry at document level is the URL, embedded in the `chrome-distiller://` host as a hash, which is address-as-identifier but deliberately one-way. The lesson is negative and sharp: proximity to the live DOM does not produce addressability; carrying the address has to be an explicit design commitment, and every tool in this batch that had the opportunity declined to make it.
adversarial_exposure: The least exposed extractor in this batch on concealed content, and for exactly the reason this project's constraints forbid: it reads layout. Its hidden-element removal runs against a live DOM with computed style available, so stylesheet-class concealment, visibility:hidden applied from an external sheet, and zero-size elements are filterable in a way no static parser can match, and the importance scoring uses image dimensions and page position, which further penalises off-screen and degenerate-size content. It is therefore the empirical counterexample to any claim that layout-blind folds are not at a concealment disadvantage -- DOM Distiller demonstrates the gap is real and that closing it is what geometry buys. Residual exposures remain: text coloured to match the background, text behind an opacity trick or a clip-path, and content covered by another element are all still visible to it, since none of those change the element's own geometry. And it inherits the deletion-volume accident: it drops most of the page, so most payloads land outside the kept region -- inverting for a payload placed in the article body. The honest summary for this project: a layout-blind fold IS structurally more exposed than DOM Distiller, and the mitigation has to come from somewhere other than pretending otherwise -- provenance plus a peripheral geometry channel read by the actuator, not by the fold.
provenance_carrying: Document-level only, and partly encoded rather than stated. DomDistillerResult carries the title, the pagination_info (next/prev URLs), content_images, timing and debug fields; the source URL is present via the distilled-page scheme and via metadata extraction. There is nothing per token, per element or per node: no xpath, no offsets, no capture timestamp field, no shadow depth (concept absent), no gate state. The distiller is nonetheless the closest any tool here comes to having the RAW MATERIAL for real provenance -- it runs in-page with live node identity, the URL, the clock, and the security level all in hand -- and it carries essentially none of it into the output. That is the single most direct confirmation available that per-token provenance is a design commitment rather than a technical obstacle, which is the argument this project's `url : xpath : markdown : content` key already makes.
roundtrip_safety: Not a fixed point and not testable in the usual way, because the output lives at a scheme where the distiller does not re-run. Conceptually, re-distilling distilled output would fail for the same reason it fails elsewhere: the class names, container contrasts and -- decisively here -- the page positions and image dimensions that the scorer reads have all been replaced by the distiller's own template geometry, so the second pass scores a different document entirely. The layout dependence makes round-tripping strictly worse than for static extractors: even the same input is not a fixed point across viewports. Escaping policy is HTML sanitization for safe rendering, with mixed-content and cert-error subresources blocked; it is a rendering-safety policy, not a lossless-serialization policy, and no round-trip guarantee is claimed or implied.
token_budget_and_ordering: No budget concept and no ordering contract, but a genuinely distinctive ordering INPUT that nothing else here has: relative page position is a scoring feature, so the distiller's notion of importance is partly spatial, and its output order is document order among elements it judged important by (among other things) where they sit. That is the germ of a real ordering contract -- 'rank by position, not just by document order' -- and it is available only to a layout-aware component. In this project's architecture that maps cleanly onto the peripheral: geometry keyed by address, read by an actuator, could produce a position-derived ORDERING for the fold's output without geometry ever entering the fold's keep/discard decision. That separation is the adoptable form of the idea and is precisely what the no_layout_in_the_fold constraint permits. Past the 50%-context-fill recency-dominance threshold, having any principled ordering signal at all is worth more than a marginally better extraction.
representation_cost: Comparable to Readability on articles -- roughly 5-20% of source token count -- with images retained (and thus image tokens, if the consumer is multimodal) and pagination allowing the distilled artifact to be LARGER than the source page when a multi-page article is stitched. That last property is unique in this batch and worth naming: it is the only extractor that can produce more content than the single input document contained, because it follows next-page links. What is bought per token saved is the usual total loss of affordances, state, addressability and shadow content, plus, uniquely, a dependence on viewport that means the token count itself is not stable across devices.
what_could_be_adopted: Four mechanisms, one of them the most valuable single idea in the extraction half of this batch. (1) THE SEPARATE DISTILLABILITY GATE. Splitting 'can this be done well?' from 'do it', with the gate able to refuse outright, converts silent quality failure into explicit refusal. It is architecturally cheap, it is orthogonal to the extraction algorithm, and it is exactly the loud-failure discipline this project's no-mocks posture already demands elsewhere. Adopt the SHAPE, not its features -- its URL-substring heuristics are a structure_agnosticism violation to be refused explicitly. (2) POSITION-DERIVED ORDERING AS A PERIPHERAL. Relative page position as an ordering signal, computed by an actuator from the geometry peripheral keyed by address, feeding the fold's output ORDER while never touching its keep/discard decision -- the constraint-compliant way to get the one thing layout genuinely buys. (3) THE `chrome-distiller://` HOST CONSTRUCTION: random string plus URL hash, so a derived artifact's identifier is neither guessable nor cross-linkable. That is a ready-made pattern for naming stored captures without making the store enumerable. (4) THE SECURITY GATE: refusing to produce an artifact for non-SECURE pages, and refusing mixed-content and cert-error subresources, is a stored-artifact hygiene rule with no analogue in any other tool here and it is trivially portable. What must NOT be adopted: geometry inside the classification, the boilerpipe density scoring, the URL-shape page typing, and the codebase itself, which is archived and built on a dead toolchain.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: REJECTED, twice over and more severely than any other item in this batch. The distiller labels elements content/not-content -- naming regions -- and the distillability gate types pages from URL SUBSTRINGS ('forum', '.php', 'index') and from Open Graph/AMP markers, which is region-and-kind naming from the address itself. For a project whose trie key contains `url`, this is the specific adjacent temptation worth writing down and refusing. no_layout_in_the_fold: REJECTED, and this is the item's defining violation. Geometry is not a peripheral here -- relative page position and image dimensions are scoring features INSIDE the keep/discard decision, computed style is read during hidden-element removal, and the whole pipeline is triggered by compositor layout events. It is the exact architecture the constraint forbids, which makes it the definitive NEGATIVE ORACLE for it: it quantifies what layout-in-the-fold buys (better concealment filtering, size-aware decisions) and what it costs (viewport-dependent output, no cross-version determinism, no reproducibility, whole-page recomputation per relayout). o_delta: REJECTED, and instructively so -- an incremental TRIGGER (layout events) driving WHOLESALE recomputation, 1-3 times per load, is the precise anti-pattern an O(delta) claim must not resemble. Geometric dependence additionally makes content-free changes cost-bearing. no_mocks: NEUTRAL-to-POSITIVE in principle -- no learned model in the distiller path, real browser required by construction, so it cannot be stubbed -- but its distillability gate does use a trained classifier whose model and training data are unpublished, an unauditable component in a measured path. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY. It never patches attachShadow, so it does not violate the rule; but running in-page against a live DOM it had every opportunity to traverse OPEN shadow roots and does not, and emits no unreachable marker -- so it silently returns near-empty distillations on component-heavy pages while reporting success. That is the dishonest-coverage failure the constraint exists to prevent, demonstrated by the tool best positioned to avoid it. OVERALL VERDICT: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY. Not adoptable as a component (archived, unbuildable, layout-fused), but the highest-value negative control in the batch, with the refusal gate, the position-as-peripheral-ordering idea, the artifact-naming scheme and the security gate all extractable as design patterns.
governance_signal_handling: None as an extractor, and the browser's own handling is the only thing in play. DOM Distiller reads no robots.txt, honours no Content Signals or ai.txt directive, implements no IETF AIPREF vocabulary, presents no Web Bot Auth signature, and has no HTTP 402 path -- it operates on a page the user has already loaded in their own session, which is the governance-favourable case and the same case this project is in. The one governance-adjacent behaviour it does implement is the SecurityLevel::SECURE gate, which is a transport-security policy rather than an access-permission one. Worth noting for this project: operating strictly downstream of a page the user loaded themselves is the strongest governance position available, and it should be stated as a design property rather than left implicit, because it is what distinguishes a sensor from a crawler under every one of these emerging signalling schemes.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The distiller retains nothing persistently on its own -- Reader Mode is a view, not a store -- and that is a materially better default than any extractor here whose output is written to disk. Where storage happens (the iOS Reading List, offline saving), the stored artifact is the regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, and what gets stored is the distilled article plus its images plus scraped author/date metadata, with no gate-state marker and no capture timestamp in the result structure. Comments are excluded by the extraction, which removes the largest UGC/PII surface as a side effect of the article-only design -- an accidental data-minimisation win worth naming, since it is the same posture Trafilatura reaches only via an explicit switch. The unresolved exposure is the overlay-capture failure mode: a distillation that captured a login or consent overlay may store text from an authenticated context, indistinguishable in the artifact from public page content. [uncertain] on whether any current Chrome configuration performs server-side distillation, which would change the disclosure analysis entirely.
